title: San Francisco earthquake (M7.9)
summary: The earthquake and the fire that followed destroyed much of San Francisco. Many California cities had building codes by then, but none of them considered earthquake forces.
significance: This is where earthquake engineering in California starts, but not regulation. No statewide seismic rule and no engineering license followed for another two decades, and anyone could still design a building.
sources: Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: Santa Barbara earthquake (M6.8)
summary: Thirteen people died and most of the downtown commercial district was destroyed. The Sheffield Dam above the city also failed.
significance: Santa Barbara rewrote its building code that year to require design for horizontal forces, the first such requirement in California, and Palo Alto followed in 1926. The earthquake was also a catalyst for the first Uniform Building Code two years later.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1925 Santa Barbara earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/1925-santa-barbara-earthquake/>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: First Uniform Building Code
summary: West Coast building officials published the first edition of the Uniform Building Code. Its earthquake provisions sat in an appendix "for optional use", which cities could choose whether to adopt.
significance: The UBC was the model code for the western states for the next seventy years, and California's structural engineers would later write its seismic chapters. In 1927, though, designing for earthquakes was still optional almost everywhere. That appendix became mandatory for one building type six years later, when the state adopted it as the design standard for public schools under the Field Act.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1925 Santa Barbara earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/1925-santa-barbara-earthquake/>; R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>

title: St. Francis Dam failure
summary: A 200-foot concrete dam built for the Los Angeles water system under William Mulholland gave way and sent a flood down the Santa Clara River valley to the sea. The Board's own history puts the dead at 409 to 450. Inspection afterward found the dam anchored to weak, faulted rock.
significance: This is the reason California licenses engineers at all. The Legislature concluded that unregulated design of public works was a hazard to the public, and passed the Civil Engineers Act the following year. It also passed a dam safety law in 1929 whose model of state plan review and inspection was copied four years later for schools.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>; R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>

title: Structural engineers organize
summary: Twelve consulting structural engineers founded the Structural Engineers Association of Southern California at the University Club in Los Angeles. A northern association followed in 1930, and the two formed a statewide association (SEAOC) that held its first convention in December 1932.
significance: Interest in earthquake design after Santa Barbara was one reason the associations formed, and they gave structural engineers a collective voice two years before the title existed. They went on to write the state's seismic design provisions and, for decades, to supply the engineers who wrote and graded the structural exam.
sources: SEAOSC, Identity and Origin <https://www.seaoc.org/seaosc-identity-and-origin>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994); R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>

title: Civil Engineers Act: California starts licensing engineers
summary: Assembly Bill 174 (Chapter 801, Statutes of 1929) created the Board of Registration for Civil Engineers, and registration began on August 14, 1929. The bill started as a registration law for all engineers, but mining, mechanical and electrical engineers objected and were written out, so it covered civil engineers only.
significance: Civil engineering became a practice act: you need the license to do the work. Every Structural Engineer license since has been issued on top of a Civil Engineer license, which is why structural engineers are always a subset of California's civil engineers.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>; NSPE-California, Inception of the California Professional Engineers Act <https://nspe-calif.org/inception-of-the-california-professional-engineers-act/>

title: The Structural Engineer title is created
summary: As buildings got taller, architects and engineers disputed who could design their structures. Structural engineers wanted a practice act of their own, sought the architects' support, and did not get one. The compromise was a title: a registered civil engineer whom the Board found qualified in structural engineering could call themselves a structural engineer (Chapter 254, Statutes of 1931). The northern association led the effort, with San Francisco engineer H. J. Brunnier doing much of the work.
significance: California became the second state, after Illinois in 1915, to recognize structural engineers separately. The law protected the name and not the work, and reserved no class of building for those who held it. Two arguments were lost along the way: that the title should also cover bridge designers, and that it should hang from the architect's license rather than the civil engineer's. A title layered on the civil license is still how it works.
data_note: License No. 1 is dated November 12, 1931. Numbers reached about 240 by June 1932 and about 370 by January 1933, faster than exam sittings alone could produce, which suggests the first holders were established engineers approved on their record. Fewer than one in ten of those 1930s licenses survive in the public data, so the earliest bars on the Time tab understate what was issued. One SEAOC account dates the title to 1932; the Board's statute citation and the first license date both point to 1931.
chart_note: Registered civil engineers found qualified in structural engineering may use the title. License No. 1 is dated November 12, 1931.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>; G. Brandow, 100 Years of Structural Engineering Licensure, STRUCTURE, Feb. 2015 <https://issuu.com/structuremag/docs/feb15/26>; R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>; This dashboard's license data

title: Long Beach earthquake (M6.4)
summary: The earthquake struck at 5:54 pm on a Friday and killed about 120 people. More than 70 schools were destroyed and 120 more damaged, roughly three quarters of the schools in the area, a few hours after children had gone home. It was also the first earthquake captured by strong-motion instruments.
significance: No other event did more to define what a California structural engineer is for. Within a month the Legislature passed the Field Act, and the Riley Act soon after. Henry Degenkolb, who started work in 1936, learned his trade from the engineers who had inspected the damaged schools and written the new state rules.
chart_note: About 120 deaths; three quarters of the area's schools destroyed or damaged. Led to the Field and Riley Acts.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1933 Long Beach earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/longbeachearthquake/>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994); R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>

title: Field Act: public schools need an architect or structural engineer
summary: Assemblymember Don C. Field, a building contractor from Glendale, introduced the bill 13 days after Long Beach, and the governor signed it on April 10 (Chapter 59, Statutes of 1933). Drafted over a weekend from the 1929 dam safety law, it put the design and construction of public schools under state supervision. Plans must be prepared by a licensed architect or structural engineer, checked by the state before construction, and built under continuous independent inspection.
significance: This was the first law to reserve a class of buildings for holders of the structural title, and it gave a two-year-old title real value. Architects tried to block it in the Senate because it obliged them to hire structural engineers; the structural engineers association backed it. The state then advertised for structural engineers to check plans and examine existing schools, which gave the profession steady work through the Depression. The Seismic Safety Commission reports that no Field Act school has collapsed in an earthquake since.
chart_note: Public school plans must come from a licensed architect or structural engineer and be checked by the state.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: Field Act <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/field-act/>; Seismic Safety Commission, The Field Act and Public School Construction (2007) <https://www.ssc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2020/08/cssc_2007-03_field_act_report.pdf>; Education Code section 17302 <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=EDC&sectionNum=17302>; R. Olson, Legislative Politics and Seismic Safety: California's Early Years and the Field Act, Earthquake Spectra 19(1), 2003 <https://mitigation.eeri.org/files/Olson_Legislative_Politics_CA.pdf>

title: Riley Act: every new building designed for lateral force
summary: Passed weeks after the Field Act, the Riley Act required every local government to have a building department and required new buildings to resist a horizontal force equal to 2 percent of their weight.
significance: This was the first statewide seismic design requirement for ordinary buildings. Enforcement was thin at first because local departments were understaffed, but it made lateral-force design a routine part of practice.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1933 Long Beach earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/longbeachearthquake/>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>; Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>

title: Garrison Act: older schools must be evaluated
summary: The Field Act covered only new construction. The Garrison Act required districts to have their pre-1933 school buildings examined and to fix or replace the unsafe ones. The Greene Acts of 1967 and 1968 finally set a deadline, barring unsafe buildings from school use after June 1975.
significance: Evaluating and replacing pre-Field Act schools was steady work for structural engineers for four decades. It also set the pattern of state-mandated evaluation of existing buildings that later reached hospitals and unreinforced masonry.
sources: D. Barclay, The Field Act: History and Issues for California Schools <https://suekayton.com/dan/FieldAct.pdf>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: El Centro (Imperial Valley) earthquake
summary: Nine people died and most buildings in Imperial and Brawley were damaged. An instrument at El Centro recorded the shaking, and that record was the main basis for seismic design standards for decades.
significance: For a generation of structural engineers, the El Centro record was the earthquake they designed for. It helped turn seismic design from a rule of thumb into something that could be calculated and tested.
sources: Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>

title: Other engineering branches are registered
summary: Legislation registered chemical, electrical, mechanical and petroleum engineers by title, and the Board became the State Board of Registration for Civil and Professional Engineers. In 1967 electrical and mechanical engineering were converted to practice acts.
significance: Structural was no longer the only specialty title. It remained, until the geotechnical title of 1982, the only one that required a prior civil license and a second examination. Degenkolb, looking back in 1985, thought the growing list of branches and the grandfathering that came with each had diluted what registration meant.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>; NCEES, History of the National Council (2020) <https://ncees.org/wp-content/uploads/2020_history_web_revised.pdf>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994); NSPE-California, Inception of the California Professional Engineers Act <https://nspe-calif.org/inception-of-the-california-professional-engineers-act/>

title: San Francisco's "Vensano" code
summary: San Francisco adopted a building code with higher earthquake coefficients than Los Angeles used, championed by public works director Harry Vensano. Most northern California engineers thought the numbers too high and fought the code before the Board of Supervisors, who sided with Vensano.
significance: Degenkolb, then a young engineer, remembered the fights as bitter and settled by laymen rather than on technical grounds. The local engineering societies responded by appointing the joint committee that wrote "Separate 66", and the 1955 San Francisco code that came out of it had everyone's backing.
sources: Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: "Separate 66": Lateral Forces of Earthquake and Wind
summary: A ten-member joint committee of ASCE's San Francisco section and the northern structural engineers published a method that tied a building's design earthquake force to its period of vibration instead of its number of stories.
significance: Critics called it oversimplified, but the idea is still the basis of how buildings are analyzed for lateral force. It also exposed that north and south were designing to different rules, which prompted the statewide committee that wrote the Blue Book.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: SEAOC Blue Book <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/seaoc-bluebook/>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: Kern County (Tehachapi) earthquake
summary: Tehachapi and Arvin were hit hard and twelve people died. Old and poorly built buildings cracked and collapsed, while damage to well-designed structures was slight.
significance: It was the first strong test of construction built since the 1933 laws, and the results supported the lateral-force approach. Degenkolb was among the engineers in the field parties that examined the damage.
sources: Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: SEAOC Blue Book, first edition
summary: A statewide committee of SEAOC volunteers published its Recommended Lateral Force Requirements, known from its cover as the Blue Book. Lateral-force rules in the codes of the day were thin and inconsistent, and the Blue Book quickly became the de facto standard.
significance: For the next forty years the Uniform Building Code took its earthquake provisions almost verbatim from this document, so California's structural engineers were in effect writing the seismic code for the western United States. Its influence faded only when the national International Building Code replaced the UBC in 2000.
data_note: The 1,000th structural title was issued in March 1959, twenty-eight years after the first.
chart_note: SEAOC's Recommended Lateral Force Requirements became the basis of the UBC's seismic provisions.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: SEAOC Blue Book <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/seaoc-bluebook/>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: San Fernando (Sylmar) earthquake (M6.6)
summary: Fifty-eight people died, most of them in the collapse of buildings at the Veterans Administration hospital in Sylmar. The nearly new Olive View hospital was wrecked and freeway overpasses fell.
significance: Modern, code-designed buildings had failed, which discredited the codes of the 1960s. The state responded with the Hospital Seismic Safety Act, fault zoning and a strong-motion instrument program. The profession set up the Applied Technology Council to rework seismic design, and the 1976 Uniform Building Code followed.
chart_note: 58 deaths; hospital and freeway collapses. Led to the Hospital Seismic Safety Act and the 1976 UBC.
sources: Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>; SEAONC Legacy Project: 1971 San Fernando earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/sanfernandoearthquake/>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: Hospital Seismic Safety Act: hospitals need a structural engineer
summary: Senate Bill 519 (Alquist) was signed in December 1972 and took effect on March 7, 1973. Modeled on the Field Act, it put hospital design and construction under state review and set special building standards. The law requires a structural engineer to prepare and sign the structural design.
significance: Hospitals became the second building type reserved for structural engineers. Public schools and hospitals are still the only two. A 2015 legislative review confirmed that everything else may be designed by a civil engineer.
chart_note: Hospital structural design is reserved to structural engineers. Effective March 7, 1973.
sources: Hospital Facilities Seismic Safety Act (Wikipedia) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_Facilities_Seismic_Safety_Act>; Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>; Health and Safety Code section 129805 <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=129805>; Senate 2015 sunset background paper <https://archive.senate.ca.gov/sites/archive.senate.ca.gov/files/committees/2015-16/sbp.senate.ca.gov/sites/sbp.senate.ca.gov/files/Board%20of%20Professional%20Engineers%20background.pdf>

title: 1976 Uniform Building Code
summary: The first edition to absorb the lessons of San Fernando. It raised earthquake design forces, added factors for site soil and for a building's importance, and built on the ductile concrete detailing introduced a few years earlier.
significance: The 1976 code is the dividing line between older and modern construction. Later laws and retrofit programs use it as their benchmark. A 1999 school-safety law, for example, targeted buildings that do not meet it.
sources: Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: Geotechnical Engineer: a second title authority
summary: The Legislature added the Geotechnical Engineer title on the same pattern as the structural title: a civil license first, then further experience and a further examination (Chapter 646, Statutes of 1982). In the same period, civil engineers licensed after January 1, 1982 lost the automatic authority to practice land surveying.
significance: It confirmed the structural title as California's template for a specialty within civil engineering. Structural and geotechnical are still the only two title authorities in engineering.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>

title: Grading on the curve ends
summary: National examiners replaced norm-referenced scoring of the professional engineering exam with a fixed passing standard in 1985, and California's Board made the same change. Interviewed that November, Henry Degenkolb said the pass rate on the first exam graded the new way fell from over 30 percent to about 10 percent. The Board also began using advisory committees of senior engineers to check that applicants had the experience they claimed.
significance: Under a curve, a fixed share of each sitting passed however well prepared the group was. With a fixed standard, the number of new licenses could swing sharply from one year to the next, and it has ever since.
data_note: Only 26 structural licenses were issued in February 1985, against 93 a year earlier and 148 in March 1986. Degenkolb does not say which exam he meant, but the structural numbers move the way he described.
chart_note: Exams move from grading on a curve to a fixed passing standard. Only 26 structural licenses were issued in February 1985.
sources: NCEES, History of the National Council (2020) <https://ncees.org/wp-content/uploads/2020_history_web_revised.pdf>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994); This dashboard's license data

title: First national structural exams
summary: The national council offered its first separate structural exam, Structural I, in fall 1985, and added Structural II in fall 1987. They were meant for states that authorize structural engineers after general registration. California kept its own 16-hour, state-written structural exam.
significance: From here there were two tracks: a national exam most states could use, and the state-written exams of California, Washington and Illinois. Reconciling them took another twenty-five years. Degenkolb recalled the California exams of his day as sixteen hours of civil and sixteen of structural, open book, and demanding.
exam_format: Structural I: 8 hours. Structural II: 8 hours of essay problems. California: 16-hour state-written exam.
chart_note: NCEES Structural I first offered in fall 1985 and Structural II in fall 1987. California keeps its own 16-hour exam.
sources: NCEES, History of the National Council (2020) <https://ncees.org/wp-content/uploads/2020_history_web_revised.pdf>; G. Brandow, Status of Structural Engineering (NCEES task force slides) <https://www.selicensure.org/sites/default/files/pdf/research/8-GEB-NCEES.pdf>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: Unreinforced Masonry Building Law
summary: Senate Bill 547 required local governments in the state's highest seismic zone to inventory their unreinforced masonry buildings and set up programs to reduce the hazard by 1990. It reached 286 jurisdictions and more than 25,000 buildings.
significance: This was the first statewide law aimed at privately owned existing buildings. Local retrofit ordinances followed over the next decade, and with them a large volume of evaluation and strengthening work.
sources: Living Where the Earth Shakes (California Senate Office of Research, 2000) <https://sor.senate.ca.gov/sites/sor.senate.ca.gov/files/Living%20Where%20the%20Earth%20Shakes.pdf>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: Seismic and surveying exams added for every civil engineer
summary: Starting with the April 1988 sitting, every applicant for a California civil license had to pass state exams in seismic principles and engineering surveying in addition to the national civil exam.
significance: A civil engineer can legally design most buildings, yet the national civil exam did not test earthquake design. Degenkolb had called that a mistake in 1985, noting that out-of-state engineers were admitted on a one-hour or oral earthquake test he considered a token. The new exam raised the floor under the structural title: every structural engineer licensed since has already passed a seismic exam as a civil engineer.
chart_note: All civil applicants must pass California seismic principles and engineering surveying exams.
sources: Business and Professions Code section 6755.1 <https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=6755.1>; BPELSG, History of the Board <https://www.bpelsg.ca.gov/about_us/history.pdf>; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: Experience and references for the title go into regulation
summary: In 1988 and 1989 the Board drafted regulations defining what counts as qualifying experience for the structural title and what professional references an applicant must supply (Title 16, sections 426.12 and 427.30). The Board then had thirteen members, seven of them members of the public.
significance: Degenkolb described a system that had leaned on references from engineers who knew the candidate, and one that stopped working as the state grew. These rules turned the custom into a written standard, and they are the origin of today's requirement for documented structural experience in responsible charge.
data_note: The structural exam was then given once a year in August (August 12 in 1989), with results that winter. That is why most licenses of this period carry December, January or February dates.
sources: California Regulatory Law Reporter, Vol. 9, No. 3 (Summer 1989), p. 68; Henry J. Degenkolb, Connections: The EERI Oral History Series (EERI, 1994)

title: 1988 Uniform Building Code adopted statewide
summary: California adopted the 1988 Uniform Building Code effective July 1, 1989, and for the first time applied one model code to every occupancy and state agency. The 1988 edition rewrote the earthquake base-shear equation around response modification factors drawn from the Applied Technology Council's ATC 3-06 study.
significance: This is the form of seismic design engineers still use: an elastic force reduced by a factor for how much damage the structural system can tolerate. Engineers examined after this learned a different procedure from those licensed before.
chart_note: One model code for all occupancies; base shear rewritten around response modification factors.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1988 Uniform Building Code <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/88ubc/>

title: Loma Prieta earthquake (M6.9)
summary: The largest Bay Area earthquake since 1906 killed 63 people. The upper deck of the Cypress freeway in Oakland collapsed, a section of the Bay Bridge fell, and soft-story apartment buildings failed in San Francisco's Marina District.
significance: It exposed existing buildings and bridges rather than new ones. Caltrans began a statewide bridge retrofit program, San Francisco passed its unreinforced masonry ordinance in 1992, and the Bay Bridge's east span was eventually replaced, opening in September 2013. Retrofit became a large share of structural practice.
chart_note: 63 deaths; Cypress freeway and Bay Bridge failures. Start of large-scale retrofit programs.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/loma-prieta-earthquake/>

title: Northridge earthquake (M6.7)
summary: Fifty-seven people died. Welded connections fractured in many steel moment-frame buildings, a system that had been considered highly reliable, and a parking structure built in the early 1990s collapsed at Cal State Northridge.
significance: The connection failures led to years of testing and new rules for pre-qualified connections, and the 1997 code added near-fault and redundancy factors. The state also passed SB 1953 to force the retrofit of older hospitals. Public schools built under the Field Act came through without a collapse.
chart_note: 57 deaths; steel moment-frame connection fractures. Led to new connection rules and SB 1953.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1994 Northridge earthquake <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/northridge-earthquake/>; Seismic Safety Commission, The Field Act and Public School Construction (2007) <https://www.ssc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/5/2020/08/cssc_2007-03_field_act_report.pdf>

title: SB 1953: older hospitals must be retrofitted
summary: Signed eight months after Northridge, the bill extended hospital seismic law to buildings that predated the 1973 act. Acute-care buildings had to stop posing a significant risk to life by 2008 and be capable of operating after an earthquake by 2030.
significance: About half of California's hospitals were affected. Because hospital structural design is reserved to structural engineers, the law created one of the largest sustained bodies of work tied directly to the license.
sources: Hospital Facilities Seismic Safety Act (Wikipedia) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hospital_Facilities_Seismic_Safety_Act>; Stanford University, Evolution of Codes <https://quake06.stanford.edu/10-evolution-codes>

title: 1997 Uniform Building Code: the last UBC
summary: The 1997 edition took effect in California on July 1, 1999. Responding to Northridge, it moved seismic design to a strength basis and added near-fault factors, a redundancy factor and limits on irregular structures in high-seismic regions.
significance: It was the last edition of the code California's engineers had shaped for forty years. Its successor, the International Building Code of 2000, merged the three regional model codes into one national document.
chart_note: The last UBC: strength design, near-fault factors and a redundancy factor.
sources: SEAONC Legacy Project: 1997 Uniform Building Code <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/97ubc/>

title: California's structural exam goes half national
summary: Through 2003 California wrote its own 16-hour structural exam. From 2004 candidates took the national Structural II exam, eight hours of essay problems, plus an eight-hour California exam (often called SE III) that kept the state's seismic emphasis.
significance: It was the first time part of the California structural exam came from outside the state, and it made the license easier to compare with other states'. Washington had adopted the same arrangement in 1998.
exam_format: NCEES Structural II: 8 hours, four essay problems. California SE III: 8 hours, multiple choice and essay.
chart_note: NCEES Structural II plus an 8-hour California exam replace the state-written 16-hour exam.
sources: G. Brandow, Status of Structural Engineering (NCEES task force slides) <https://www.selicensure.org/sites/default/files/pdf/research/8-GEB-NCEES.pdf>; BPELSG Structural Engineer exam FAQ (rev. 2/2024) <https://www.bpelsg.ca.gov/applicants/se_faqs.pdf>

title: California adopts the International Building Code
summary: The 2007 California Building Code, based on the 2006 International Building Code and ASCE 7-05, took effect on January 1, 2008 and ended the state's use of the Uniform Building Code.
significance: Seismic design moved from provisions written largely in California to national standards. A national task force on structural licensing, set up in 2001 and chaired by a California engineer, had already concluded that one building code in every state called for one structural exam.
chart_note: The 2007 California Building Code, based on the 2006 IBC, replaces the UBC.
sources: 2007 California Building Code (California Building Standards Commission); SEAONC Legacy Project: 1997 Uniform Building Code <https://legacy.seaonc.org/event/97ubc/>; G. Brandow, 100 Years of Structural Engineering Licensure, STRUCTURE, Feb. 2015 <https://issuu.com/structuremag/docs/feb15/26>

title: The Board becomes BPELSG
summary: The Board for Geologists and Geophysicists was abolished in October 2009 and its duties moved to the engineers' board, which was renamed the Board for Professional Engineers, Land Surveyors, and Geologists on January 1, 2011.
significance: An administrative change, but it is why structural engineer records now sit in a public feed that also covers land surveyors and geologists, and why this dashboard has to filter them out.
sources: BPELSG 2023 Sunset Review Report, Section 1 <https://abp.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2024-03/sunsetreport2023bpelsg.pdf>

title: A single national 16-hour structural exam
summary: The national council replaced Structural I and II with one 16-hour exam, first given in April 2011: eight hours on vertical forces and eight on lateral forces, each with a breadth session and a depth session. Until then California, Oregon and Washington had each added their own exams to the national one. California's Board found that the new exam met all the requirements for licensure, and that year's sunset bill (SB 543) removed the state-specific structural exam from the law.
significance: For the first time since 1931, a California structural license rested entirely on an exam written outside the state. It also put California on the same exam as every other state that licenses structural engineers, which simplified licensing across state lines.
data_note: The years around the switch are the busiest in the record: 186 licenses in 2010, 129 in 2011, 231 in 2012 and 169 in 2013. 2012 is the largest single year in the data.
exam_format: Two 8-hour components (vertical forces, lateral forces), each with a breadth session and a depth session in buildings or bridges.
chart_note: The NCEES 16-hour exam replaces Structural I and II, and California drops its state-specific structural exam.

title: SEAOC's "significant structures" proposal
summary: SEAOC proposed that newly licensed civil engineers no longer be allowed to design "significant structures" such as fire and police stations, hazardous-material facilities and water storage, reserving them for structural engineers. The proposal was taken up in the Board's 2015 sunset review and discussed with the other engineering associations, and the Board reported back to the Legislature in 2016. No bill followed.
significance: This is the most recent attempt to turn the 1931 title into a restriction on practice. Washington's significant-structures law took effect in 2008, and Utah has one too. Both let engineers already practicing structural design move to the new license without another exam, and SEAOC's proposal likewise protected engineers already licensed. Oregon and Nevada have similar rules, and Illinois and Hawaii reserve nearly all structures. In California the reserved list is still public schools and hospitals.

title: The structural exam goes computer-based
summary: The last pencil-and-paper exam was given in October 2023. Since April 2024 the exam has been delivered at test centers in four separately scored sections: breadth and depth for vertical forces, and breadth and depth for lateral forces. It grew from 16 hours over two days to about 21 hours over four sittings. Breadth sections are offered year-round and depth sections twice a year, with depth results taking 10 to 13 weeks. California now requires the exam to be passed before an application is filed.
significance: Hand-written essay solutions, the core of the structural exam for generations, are gone. In 2022 the Council of American Structural Engineers warned that the longer, costlier format could deter younger engineers, and noted that every other national exam had lost candidates when it moved to computer. First-time pass rates published in mid-2026 were about 45 percent on the breadth sections and 54 to 63 percent on the buildings depth sections, but a candidate must clear all four.
data_note: New licenses fell to 71 in 2024 and 62 in 2025, the lowest annual totals since 2002, after averaging about 135 a year from 2021 to 2023.
exam_format: Four computer-based sections. Breadth: 55 multiple-choice questions in 5.5 hours. Depth: scenario-based, with alternative item types. Closed book, with an electronic handbook and design standards supplied.
chart_note: Four computer-based sections replace the paper exam. New licenses fall to 71 in 2024 and 62 in 2025.
